# The Oxbow

Rivers are restless about their own paths. A river bends, and the outside of each bend gets eaten away by the current while the inside collects sand and silt. The loops grow tighter and more exaggerated over years, until two points of land on either side of a meander are only a few meters apart. Then, during a flood, the water cuts straight across the neck of land. The river takes the shortcut, the loop is abandoned, and it slowly seals itself off into a crescent of still water called an oxbow lake.

I find these lakes oddly moving. Nothing dramatic happens to them. The river simply stops visiting. Water that was once the river's body settles into a quiet, curved pond, with reeds at the edges and herons standing in it. Over decades it fills with sediment and becomes a meadow, and eventually a faint curve in the grass is the only sign that something used to flow there.

What strikes me is that the oxbow is not a failure of the river. It is a record of the river having been somewhere. The loop was a real part of its movement, and the shortcut that replaced it was a result of that movement, not a rejection of it. Every meander shaped the land that made the next one possible.

I think about this when I consider how much of any life is oxbow: the jobs we stopped doing, the cities we passed through, the versions of ourselves that the current eventually bypassed. They feel like detours when we look back, but they were the channel we were actually in at the time. They left deposits. The soil under our present ground is partly made of them.

There is a temptation to see only the straight line, the direct route the river "should" have taken. But the straight line exists because of all the bending before it. Rivers don't know where they're going in advance. They just keep following the slope of the land and the pressure of the water, and the shape of the whole thing emerges afterward, looking like it was planned.

So if you find yourself in a loop that seems to have gone nowhere, consider that it may be quietly becoming a lake: still, a little overgrown, full of its own small life, and proof that you were moving through real ground the whole time.
